title: The state of LLM: costs and capabilities
author: krsaulitis

excerpt: Between 9 and 18 November, Anthropic, Google and OpenAI released six flagship and mid-tier models between them. Every launch post claimed some benchmark crown, and after a while we stopped being able to tell which of it mattered for us. So instead of following the launches, we went back to the people who measure this stuff for a living: Epoch AI, METR, Stanford's AI Index team, economists running randomized trials, and Artificial Analysis, which is honestly the site our team opens most often when picking a model. We wanted answers to a few practical questions. How fast are LLMs actually getting cheaper, and why isn't our bill shrinking? What can the models do now that they couldn't a year ago? Who's making money? Does any of it make people more productive? And is it worth running models on our own hardware, rented or bought? Building a product on LLMs is a bet that prices, capabilities and reliability keep moving in the right direction. The last section is my own guess at how that bet plays out, and it's labelled as such. LLMs became "AI" in under four years ChatGPT launched on 30 November 2022, so it isn't even four years old. In that short time, LLMs have more or less taken over the word "AI". In February 2026 Pew asked 5,119 Americans, for the first time, which technology comes to mind first when they think of AI. 29% named chatbots, either in general or a brand like ChatGPT, and another 6% said generative AI or LLMs. Robots and science fiction got 8%. In the same survey, the share of Americans who had heard "a lot" about AI rose from 26% in 2022 to 48%. ChatGPT alone passed a billion weekly users in August 2026, and Google's Gemini passed a billion monthly users around the same time. That matters for this post because the word hides a lot. Speech recognition, computer vision, recommendation systems and plain old machine learning are AI too, and they work under very different economics. We feel this every day.
